extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evidentiary rules for measuring damages and awarding profits in patent-infringement cases, including distinctions between originals and improvements, equity vs. law remedies, and permissible proof of value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff's actual loss is the primary measure
rubrics_metrics.description: The damages are the loss actually sustained by the plaintiff as shown by the evidence; the defendant's profits are not always the measure of the plaintiff's damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts repeatedly state that damages should reflect the plaintiff's actual loss. See cases cited (Magic Rufile Co. v. Elm City Co., Birdsall v. Coolidge, etc.). Where evidence shows the plaintiff's loss, that is controlling rather than a simple measure of the defendant's gains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant's profits may be considered by the jury
rubrics_metrics.description: The profit made by the defendant and that lost by the plaintiff are among elements the jury may consider in arriving at damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Juries may consider the defendant's gain alongside plaintiff's losses (e.g., Philp v. Nock). But such profits are not an automatic or exclusive measure without supporting evidence that ties them to plaintiff's loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant's profits measure plaintiff's loss only when plaintiff could have supplied the market
rubrics_metrics.description: The defendant's profits are the measure of the plaintiff's damages only when the invention is such that the plaintiff was ready and able to supply the market with his products, permitting the inference he would have sold all that the defendant sold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishing that the plaintiff had capacity/facilities and would have made the sales is necessary to infer damages from defendant's sales/profits. Consider equality of manufacturing facilities and previous market control (Gould's Mfg. Co. v. Cowing, Zane v. Peck Brothers).

rubrics_metrics.name: When plaintiff had prior control of the market, inference of lost sales is fair
rubrics_metrics.description: If the plaintiff had a previous control of the market, it may be inferred that those who bought from the defendant would have bought from the plaintiff but for the infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior market control and prior customers buying from the plaintiff before infringement support the presumption that defendant's sales displaced plaintiff's sales (examples: Gould's Mfg. Co. v. Cowing; Creamery v. Bowers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not include benefits derived before patent issue
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of the advantage received by the defendant must be calculated for the entire period of the infringement, but must not include the advantage which the defendant may have gained by any use of the invention before the issue of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude pre-issue gains from the damages calculation; value measured for infringement period only (text discussion and citations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison for gains must be against means open to the public
rubrics_metrics.description: In estimating the advantage derived by an infringer, the comparison must be instituted between the patented invention and such instruments or operations as are open to public employment; if the benefit does not exceed that obtainable by other public means, the infringer did not gain and the patentee did not lose by the infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The doctrine rests on assessing the marginal benefit of the patented invention over public alternatives; if no net benefit, no recoverable gain (text discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Original invention vs. improvement distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Every invention is either an original invention or an improvement on an original. If original, its infringement involves injury commensurate with the scope of the complete invention used. If an improvement, only the improvement (not the original) belongs to the inventor, and an infringement involving original+improvement involves injury commensurate only with the scope of the improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an improvement is used with the original, separate the value attributable to the original from that attributable to the improvement; if inseparable, other rules apply (see further entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: When improvement and original are inseparable, plaintiff may recover whole advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: If the old device is now never used without the improvement, or the process/machine was valueless without the improvement, or the plaintiff's and defendant's inventions are so confused their benefits cannot be separated, the whole advantage gained is imputed to the plaintiff's improvement and may be taken as the measure of his loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts allow imputation of entire profits to the improvement where separation is impossible (text examples and citations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Profits in equity are the defendant's actual gains or savings
rubrics_metrics.description: Profits in equity are the gain or saving which the defendant has made by employing the infringing invention — an actual pecuniary benefit which resulted directly from the wrongful use of the plaintiff's property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equitable accounting treats the enterprise as the plaintiff's and computes gains/savings without permitting the defendant to offset by what he might lawfully have earned; items of cost/revenue must be accounted as they would have been by the rightful owner.

rubrics_metrics.name: At law, defendant's profits are only an indication of plaintiff's loss and require proof tying them to plaintiff's injury
rubrics_metrics.description: At law the profits of the defendant serve merely as an indication of the amount which the plaintiff has lost through the infringement and have no significance until it has been proved that the advantage derived by the defendant would, but for the infringement, have been enjoyed by the plaintiff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The plaintiff must prove the causal link between the defendant's gains and the plaintiff's loss; courts caution against treating defendant's whole profit as plaintiff's damage absent such proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let defendant escape liability by showing he could have obtained similar gains lawfully
rubrics_metrics.description: The defendant should not be allowed to keep wrongful gains on the ground that he might have honestly acquired an equal amount; equitable/accounting principles deny the wrong-doer retention even if similar lawful opportunities existed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to conversion/trust law: wrong-doer cannot reduce account of profits by hypothetical lawful alternatives; courts reject this as a defense to liability for profits from infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: When profits are used as measure, compute as selling price minus cost (and other deductions)
rubrics_metrics.description: When damages are measured by profits, these are the selling price less the cost of making and selling, the risk of bad debts and interest on capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow ordinary profit-accounting: deduct manufacturing cost, marketing expense, bad debts, interest. See McCormick v. Seymour, Wilbur v. Beecher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence admissible to show defendant's profits — sales, prices, costs, marketing expenses
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of the pecuniary profit received by the defendant from his use of the invention may be shown by evidence disclosing the quantity of his sales, the prices obtained, the cost of manufacture, and the expense of marketing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If products derive entire market value from the invention, difference between cost and receipts suffices; if not, need evidence to separate invention-caused increase in sales/profits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence: subsequent license/royalty payments or purchase price as admission of value
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount afterwards paid by the defendant for an equivalent invention, or for a license to use it, or as royalties upon his products, may be proved as an admission by him of its value in his business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts treat later payments/licensing as probative evidence of value, and established royalties are evidence of value though not conclusive (Wooster v. Thornton, McKeever v. United States examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence: expert and trade-witness opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The opinions of witnesses having experience in the trade are proper testimony on the value of the invention to the defendant's business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may consider (1) manufacturer's price, (2) percentage that usually makes a fair royalty, (3) judgments of competent experts familiar with sale and profit, (4) price paid by others for licenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Established royalty is evidence but not conclusive
rubrics_metrics.description: An established royalty is evidence of value but not an absolute test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where there is an established license fee previously paid, it may guide damages but courts will weigh it with other relevant evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Price for which device might sell or expense of making it are not proper sole measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither the price for which the device might sell nor the expense of making it is the proper measure of the defendant's gain from the use of the plaintiff's invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value must be based on actual profit to defendant, not intrinsic cost or theoretical sale price. The value depends on the profits the defendant actually made by its employments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Added or differential price rules when defendant's goods would otherwise have been sold at different prices
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the goods sold by the defendant would otherwise have been sold at a higher price by the plaintiff, the measure of damages is the profit the plaintiff would have received on such sales at the higher price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will account for price differentials; if defendant's sales displaced plaintiff's higher-priced sales, plaintiff is entitled to the profit he would have obtained at his price (cases cited: Hobbie v. Smith, American Saw Co. v. Emerson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages for design patents measured by excess value
rubrics_metrics.description: The measure of damages for the infringement of a design is its excess of value over any open-to-public device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For design patents, compute the additional value attributable to the patented design over devices already open to the public (Tomkinson v. Willetts Mfg. Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: If infringement is confined to part of an article, recovery is limited accordingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the infringement is confined to a part of the thing sold, the recovery must be limited accordingly; it cannot be as if the entire thing were covered by the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recovery should be proportionate to the extent of the article that embodies the patented feature (Philp v. Nock).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff may claim additional consequential damages (reputation, depressed markets, price-cutting)
rubrics_metrics.description: The defendant's goods may have been of inferior quality or the defendant may have lowered prices to obtain a market, thereby diminishing the reputation and salability of all products of the patented machine or process; such additional losses fall upon the plaintiff or his licensees and must be proved by direct evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are extra losses beyond simple supersedure and require direct proof (text discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Receipts or releases for use are admissible to reduce damages
rubrics_metrics.description: A receipt in full for the use of certain machines is admissible to lessen the damages pro tanto.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of payment/settlement for use can be used to mitigate the damages award (Burdell v. Denig example).

rubrics_metrics.name: No damages unless invention proved useful
rubrics_metrics.description: No damages are allowed unless the invention is proved to be useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility of the invention must be established as a prerequisite to recovery (text statement and citations).

rubrics_metrics.name: When defendant's process derives all its value from plaintiff's invention, profits measured by that value
rubrics_metrics.description: If the defendant's process derives all its value from the plaintiff's invention, the profits are measured by that value even though other processes equally useful were open to him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the infringing element is the source of the process's value, plaintiff may recover those profits (Whitney v. Mowry example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Where defendant's profits include improvements, those improvements' profits are not plaintiff's unless inseparable
rubrics_metrics.description: Profits due to the defendant's improvements do not form a measure of the plaintiff's damages; but if the improvements are inseparable from the benefits of the plaintiff's device, their value belongs to the plaintiff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate and exclude defendant's independent improvements unless they cannot be separated from the plaintiff's invention (Carter v. Baker; other citations).
